rounds.text: Amanta Healthcare Ltd trades below its intrinsic value, with a discounted cash flow model placing intrinsic value at Rs 188 per share against the current market price of Rs 172, providing a margin of safety [E38, E39]. This valuation discount exists despite exceptional fundamental acceleration, highlighted by a compounded profit growth of 114% over 3 years and 17% over the trailing twelve months [E18, E19], alongside a rules-based screen scoring a strong 87 out of 100 with a medium confidence buy rating [E57]. Furthermore, the operational engine is generating robust cash backing, with a cash conversion ratio of 3.20x and operating cash flow reaching Rs 48 Cr in March 2026 [E28, E29], while capital expenditure is aggressively scaling through a massive 1071.4% surge in capital work-in-progress to Rs 82 Cr [E33]. Market momentum also underscores the undervaluation, evidenced by a relative-strength rating of 91 against the Nifty 500 and a twelve-month price return of 31.3% [E44, E45]. Conceded: debt exceeds net worth with a leverage risk of 1.11x and borrowings rising to Rs 244 Cr [E31, E32].

Amanta Healthcare Ltd trades at a steep P/E multiple of 36.5x [E1], stretching to 43.2x against a sector benchmark of 30.8x [E6], while price growth exceeds profit growth by 26% as expectations run ahead of delivery [E50]. This rich valuation rests on shaky fundamental efficiency, demonstrated by a low ROE of 7.46% [E9], a median 5-year ROE of just 4% [E21], and an ROCE of 9.58% that lags behind the 11.76% sector benchmark [E10]. Financial risks are further magnified by a heavy debt-to-equity ratio of 1.11x where borrowings have climbed to Rs 244 Cr [E31, E32], driving free cash flow down to a negative Rs -32 Cr [E30] and resulting in a 0.00% dividend yield [E4]. Top-line expansion is slowing down significantly, evidenced by a sluggish 3-year compounded sales growth of only 4% [E15] and inconsistent operating margins [E26], all while institutional money flow turns negative with foreign institutions cutting their stake [E35, E37]. Conceded: the company has delivered strong 5-year profit growth of 22% [E17] alongside solid operating cash flows of Rs 48 Cr backed by a cash conversion ratio of 3.20x [E28, E29].

Conceded: Amanta Healthcare Ltd trades at a P/E of 36.5x [E1] and 43.2x against a sector benchmark of 30.8x [E6], with a 0.00% dividend yield [E4] and negative free cash flow of Rs -32 Cr [E30]. However, the valuation is fully justified by intrinsic value modeling from a discounted cash flow putting the share price at Rs 188 against a market price of Rs 172 [E38], leaving a positive margin of safety of 8.6% [E39]. Furthermore, the reverse DCF indicates that today's price implies an earnings growth rate of 16.7%, which sits just below the base case assumption of 18.0% [E40]. While the bear highlights heavy debt [E31], borrowings are funding a massive expansion phase with capital-work-in-progress up 1071.4% to Rs 82 Cr [E33]. The company's profitability is robust, backed by strong operating cash flows of Rs 48 Cr and a high cash conversion ratio of 3.20x [E29, E28]. Finally, institutional concerns over foreign holdings [E35] are offset by rising domestic institutional ownership, which increased to 12.20% from 11.34% [E36], supported by a rules-based screen scoring 87 out of 100 [E57].

Conceded: [E38], [E39], [E40]. The 8.6% margin of safety and the 16.7% reverse DCF growth assumption rely entirely on projections that are heavily contradicted by Amanta Healthcare Ltd’s actual delivery, as 3-year compounded sales growth has slumped to a mere 4% [E15]. The bull's dismissal of heavy debt is unwarranted when borrowings climbed to Rs 244 Cr [E32], pushing the debt-to-equity ratio to a precarious 1.11x where debt exceeds net worth [E31]. While operating cash flow reached Rs 48 Cr [E29], the massive capital-work-in-progress surge of 1071.4% to Rs 82 Cr [E33] severely burned free cash flow, driving it down to a negative Rs -32 Cr [E30]. Furthermore, pointing to rising domestic institutional ownership [E36] ignores the broader structural exit by foreign institutions dropping to 0.07% [E35], generating a negative money flow signal [E37]. Finally, the premium valuation of 43.2x P/E against a 30.8x sector benchmark [E6] is fundamentally unsupported by an anemic 5-year median return on equity of just 4% [E21].
